title: The omens before Janasthana
hook: a wounded sister reaches her brother's court, and an army of fourteen thousand gets ready to march
carry: shagun: a good sign for a new start
tomorrow: The promise to the sages, kept

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shurpanakha lunged at Sita, Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears, and she fled to Khara. Karma: every act is a seed.

Shurpanakha falls at her brother's feet, covered in blood. Khara rules Janasthana, the rakshasa stronghold in Dandaka, with his general Dushana. He's furious and proud, and both show. Who did this to you? Tell me, and they die today. She tells him: two young men in bark clothes, with bows, and a woman. Khara's first move is almost casual. He sends fourteen rakshasas to kill them, as his sister asks.
screen: `AT KHARA'S FEET.` → `WHO DID THIS?` → `FOURTEEN SENT TO KILL.`

segments.voice: The fourteen reach Panchavati with Shurpanakha pointing the way. Rama asks Lakshmana to stay by Sita and speaks to them first. We live here as hermits, at the sages' request. If you've come to fight, stop where you are. They don't. They hurl their spears, and Rama's arrows cut down all fourteen. Shurpanakha runs back and shames her brother: you call yourself a warrior, and you sent fourteen? Now Khara calls up his whole force: fourteen thousand rakshasas, with Dushana and Trishiras, the three-headed. And Valmiki slows down for the signs. A rain of blood. Jackals howling. The sun dimmed. Khara's left arm throbbing. Khara sees every one and marches on. At the hut, Rama sees signs too, and reads them: a great fight is coming. So he tells Lakshmana to take Sita to a cave hidden by trees. I'll face them alone. Here's the Hindu thread. Valmiki's world is full of meaning, and the epics are full of shakuna, omens: signs that something good or bad is near. The proud man ignores them. The wise one reads them, and acts with care. Hindu families still watch for good signs, and they also make them, on purpose, at every new start. That's where the word shagun comes from: shakuna, a sign. The shagun at a wedding, the money in an envelope, the sweets, the first gifts to the bride, is a good omen given by the people who love her. Many families add one rupee to the sum, a hundred and one, so it doesn't end in zero, and the blessing keeps going.
screen: `WARN FIRST.` · `A RAIN OF BLOOD, JACKALS HOWLING.` · `KHARA MARCHES PAST THE SIGNS.` · `SHAKUNA: AN OMEN.` · then, large: `SHAGUN: A GOOD SIGN, GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you're starting today: a class, a task, a conversation. Before it, do what many Hindu families do at a new start: pause, fold your hands, and ask for a good beginning. If you pray, you might say Shri Ganeshaya namah. If you don't, name one good sign you already have, someone in your corner, a little rest. Then breathe out, and begin.
Khara. Harsh by name, the rakshasa lord of Janasthana, who sends fourteen, then fourteen thousand, against Rama, with his general Dushana.
Keep this: shagun, a good sign for a new start. Khara marched past every omen. Day five hundred sixty-three, done.

original.note: Sanskrit khara: harsh, rough; also a word for a donkey. the name of Shurpanakha's brother, lord of Janasthana.

Khara.meaning: Shurpanakha's brother; his name means harsh

Dandaka.meaning: the great forest where the exiles live

Trishiras.meaning: the three-headed rakshasa in Khara's army

shakuna.meaning: an omen, a sign of what's near

shagun.meaning: a good-sign gift at a wedding or new start
